body: Jay Ritter's IPO statistics (Table 16/16b, updated 16-Feb-2026; 9,253 US operating-company IPOs 1980-2024, returns through Dec-2025, measured from first closing price, 3-year buy-and-hold incl. dividends). Average IPO: first-day return 18.9%, 3-yr BHR +19.1%, market-adjusted -20.5%, style-adjusted (size and book-to-market matched) -8.9%. By pre-IPO sales (2025$): under $10m sales -16.2% raw, -52.3% vs market; $100-500m sales +39.1% raw, -2.6% vs market, +5.4% style-adjusted. By profitability: unprofitable IPOs (3,926) -0.5% raw / -30.7% market-adjusted; profitable (5,327) +33.6% / -13.0%. Worst cell: unprofitable with sales under $100m: -10.3% raw, -40.9% vs market. Lesson: buying the average US IPO in its first 3 years is a negative-expectancy bet versus an index fund; the penalty is concentrated in small, young, loss-making issuers (the ones that look most like 'future multibaggers'). Larger, profitable IPOs roughly match style benchmarks. Edge, if any, comes from waiting for the post-IPO de-rating, lock-up expiry (typically 180 days) and the first few 10-Qs, not from subscribing.

data.lesson: Don't buy small loss-making IPOs at listing; revisit after lock-up and 2-4 public quarters.

title: US IPOs underperform for 3 years after listing; small unprofitable IPOs worst (Ritter 1980-2024)

body: From 17 false-alarm and 14 hidden-trap cases (India 21, US/global 10): (1) VERIFIABILITY OUTSIDE THE ACCOUNTS: every false alarm had a mechanism an outsider could check independently: store counts and footfall (DMart, Trent), subscribers/engagement (Netflix, Bharti), gold prices and owned-store inventory (Titan), sovereign counterparty and order book (HAL), listed investee prices (Info Edge), deliveries/factory output (Tesla). Every trap's good number could only be checked through company-supplied data (Satyam cash, Wirecard TPAs, Luckin orders, Manpasand distributors, Gitanjali group receivables). (2) CASH EVENTUALLY ARRIVED in false alarms (HAL FY21, Bharti CFO Rs 1.22 lakh cr, Netflix FCF 2020+, Reliance stake sales); in traps, cash never arrived or vanished. (3) GOVERNANCE was clean or improving in false alarms (Bharti, Tata/Titan, Bajaj, Apollo reducing pledge); traps carried governance flags (auditor exits, promoter stake falls, related-party deals, regulator action). (4) WHO TOOK THE OTHER SIDE: false-alarm dilution was bought by strong investors or the promoter; trap capital came from short-term lenders/MFs. (5) MANY FALSE ALARMS WERE ONLY HALF FALSE: high P/E stopped working at ~2x own median (DMart, Asian Paints, Pidilite, Page, Bajaj Finance, HDFC Bank all had 4-6 flat years after peak multiples) and Reliance's low ROCE capped returns. So 'flag false for the business' and 'flag false for the price' are separate verdicts. (6) Our checklist would have wrongly rejected Titan (CFO/PAT 0.62), Apollo (pledge) and HAL (receivables), and wrongly passed Vakrangee on CFO/PAT: calibrate, don't abandon.

data.half_false: high P/E bites at ~2x own median

title: What separated false alarms from hidden traps (17 vs 14 cases)
